newsitem.title: USA: CLINTON, STAFF TO DISCUSS LINE-ITEM VETO THURSDAY.
newsitem.headline: CLINTON, STAFF TO DISCUSS LINE-ITEM VETO THURSDAY.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his advisers are expected to discuss using the line-item veto on aspects of the balanced-budget legislation on Thursday, White House officials said on Wednesday.

Clinton said on Wednesday he expected to use the veto, which allows him to block parts of spending bills or to strike down narrowly targeted tax breaks, on the legislation signed into law this week that aims to balance the budget by 2002.
However, he said he had yet to be briefed on the matter by his staff and therefore had not decided which tax or spending provisions deserved to be stripped out of the legislation.
One official said the White House was studying two issues: the merits of the provisions themselves and the best strategy to combat the expected legal challenges to the veto.
"There are two sets of questions: what is good economic policy ... and what is in the interest of the presidency in terms of preserving the tool," said the official.

The line-item veto, sought by U.S. presidents for more than a century, took effect on January 1 and has already been subjected to one legal challenge this year, which was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Some analysts have argued that Clinton should use the veto where the White House will have the best chance of fending off lawsuits that are certain to be filed against it.

The White House official, however, said there were some within the administration arguing for a broad use of the veto, fearing that a narrow test case might result in a court ruling supporting only limited uses of the veto power.
"Part of the issue is can you get the broadest possible interpretation of what the authority is to use the veto," said the official. "That argues for a more expansive test case."
The official said Clinton may not make up his mind on Thursday. Under the law, the president has five working days from the signing of a piece of legislation to use the veto.
This would give him until Monday to announce whether and where he may apply the veto to the balanced-budget bills that he signed on Tuesday.
